summary:
Article 489 of Morocco's penal code criminalises "indecent acts" between persons of the same sex, with penalties of six months to three years' imprisonment. Outright International reports that the provision is enforced with wide police discretion and that arrests are arbitrary; 170 people were charged with same-sex relations in 2018. ILGA's State-Sponsored Homophobia survey lists Morocco among the countries whose law prohibits same-sex activity between consenting adults, and Human Rights Watch's April 2018 report "Audacity in Adversity" places Article 489 in an annex of statutes used across the Middle East and North Africa to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression.

The statute does not name transgender people, but it is applied to them. A January 2026 report by Cairo 52, "A Web of Violence: The Systemic Erasure of Transgender People in Morocco", draws on interviews with 17 trans and non-binary Moroccans, describes an interlocking system of legal, medical, social and economic hostility, and records Article 489 being used to arrest trans people on the basis of their gender expression. The same organisation's country review finds no legal gender recognition pathway and no specific statutory provisions governing transition, with de facto criminalisation instead running through Article 498 moral charges, gender-expression discrepancies and involuntary outing.

Police conduct documented in press reporting includes an allegation by an Instagram model in November 2024 that Moroccan police forced her to display her genitals after suspecting her of being trans. In January 2019 El Pais reported that police in Marrakesh handcuffed a cross-dressing man, Chafiq, after a minor traffic accident, that bystanders and officers filmed him, and that his identity documents were photographed and posted online; he later sought asylum in Europe. Wikipedia's account of LGBTQ rights in Morocco states that police disproportionately target people perceived to be LGBTQ and that the names of arrested individuals are publicised before trial.

Morocco has no law prohibiting discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no political party has enacted LGBTQ rights legislation. There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples. Official hostility is on the record: in 2017 the then Minister of Justice and Liberties, Mustafa Ramid, described homosexuals as "trash" in an interview, prompting local human rights associations to petition Prime Minister Othmani to investigate what they called his discriminatory and unconstitutional statements. Cairo 52 reports that the Grand Mufti opposes transition, and Outright International reports that the authorities block LGBTIQ organisations.

Healthcare access for trans people is not established in law or provision. Cairo 52 finds no gender-affirming healthcare framework, with some trans Moroccans self-medicating as a result, and records a 2021 recognition process that covers intersex people only. The same report describes a de facto prohibition on gender-affirming surgery for Moroccans while noting that the country once drew foreign patients for such operations: 1950s publicity around the French entertainer Coccinelle helped establish Casablanca as a place where certain doctors would perform sex change operations "albeit in clandestine circumstances", indicating unregulated care rather than a documented public facility. No current trans-specific healthcare access, identity-document procedure or shelter provision for trans visitors is recorded in the sources.

In April 2020 an online campaign targeted presumed gay and bisexual men, documented by Human Rights Watch. During that campaign some landlords ejected tenants who had been targeted, and sociologist Khalid Mouna noted that transgender influencer Sofia Talouni sought to "isolate young Moroccan homosexuals by breaking up their family unit"; journalist Hicham Tahir reported receiving "a hundred testimonies" from victims or witnesses, and one person allegedly committed suicide. In November 2022 a trans woman was violently beaten in Tangier; three minors and an adult were arrested over the assault. Outright International states that public identification as LGBTIQ in Morocco carries significant risk of violence and harassment.

Prosecutions have proceeded on thin evidence. In December 2007 a court in Ksar el-Kebir convicted six men under Article 489 after an online video of a private party, reported in the press as a "gay marriage", circulated; their lawyers said no evidence of prohibited conduct was presented, and the men received varying sentences on 17 December 2007. Dozens of people then marched through the streets of Ksar el-Kebir calling for their punishment. In 2016 two girls in Marrakesh were arrested after a cousin photographed them kissing and their mother complained to police; the case was postponed to December 2016, when both were acquitted, provoking the #freethegirls outcry.

In the 2018-19 Arab Barometer survey, 21% of Moroccan respondents said homosexuality is acceptable.
tangentialFactors:
The UN Human Rights Council adopted the SOGI resolution in September 2014, establishing an international human-rights scrutiny framework that applies to Morocco; the Washington Blade reported the adoption.

Human Rights Watch's 2018 regional report treats Morocco's Article 489 as one instance of a wider pattern of statutes across the Middle East and North Africa used against same-sex conduct and gender expression, and ILGA's comparative survey places Morocco in the same criminalising category as other states in the region. The Moroccan provision therefore sits inside a regional enforcement environment rather than standing alone.
localsOnly:
Moroccan citizens have no legal gender recognition pathway, and the 2021 recognition process documented by Cairo 52 covers intersex people only. There is no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, housing or services, and no legal recognition of same-sex couples.

Trans Moroccans who cannot obtain gender-affirming care through the health system report self-medicating. During the April 2020 outing campaign, landlords evicted tenants who had been targeted, and the campaign's documented effects included pressure on young people's family ties; one person allegedly took their own life.

State institutions reinforce the position: the Grand Mufti opposes transition, the authorities block LGBTIQ organisations, books on homosexuality are banned, and the school curriculum is required to emphasise "the danger and depravity of 'unnatural acts'".
outOfScopeNotes:
The January 2026 Cairo 52 report rests on interviews with 17 trans and non-binary Moroccans; its findings describe patterns reported by that group rather than a statistically representative sample.

No current official figures on prosecutions under Article 489 are published; the 170 charges cited by Outright International date from 2018. The application of Article 498 to trans people is documented by Cairo 52 without published case counts.

The November 2024 allegation that police forced a woman to display her genitals is a first-person account reported in the press and has not been independently confirmed. The reported suicide during the April 2020 outing campaign is described as alleged.

No current trans-specific healthcare access, identity-document procedure or shelter provision for trans visitors is recorded in the sources reviewed; the 1950s Casablanca reference concerns unregulated private practice, not a public facility. Details of the 2021 intersex recognition process are not set out in the sources.
